chunks: Sa'd ibn 'Abdillah narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr, from Abi 'Umarah, from al-Harith ibn al-Mughirah al-Nasri, from Abi 'Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

I said to him, 'We have wealth from agricultural produce, trade, and similar things, and I know that you have a right in them.' He said, 'Then why did we make it permissible for our Shias except to make their offspring content? And whoever is connected to my fathers, they are free from what is in their hands from our right. Let the witness convey to the absent one.'
And from him, from Abi Ja'far Ali ibn Mahziyar, who said:

I read in a book of Abi Ja'far (peace be upon him) from a man who asked him to make him free from his food and drink from the khums, so he wrote with his own hand, 'Whoever is in need of something from my right, he is free from it.'
ai.seo_question: What is the wisdom behind the Imam's right to khums and who is exempt from it?
ai.summary: In this narration from Imam al-Sadiq, the imposition of khums is framed not as a burden but as a means of spiritual purification and ensuring the well-being of the faithful's lineage, reflecting the Shia concept of 'tathir' (purification). The text clarifies that the Ahl al-Bayt's right to their share does not strip followers of their wealth, but rather sanctifies it, while also offering flexibility for those in genuine need. This highlights the pragmatic and merciful nature of Shia jurisprudence regarding financial obligations.
